extracted.intended_audience: intermediate-to-advanced fiction writers and writing-group leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for fiction craft (sentence-level choices, tense, point of view, pacing) and for selecting/using a craft workbook or running critique groups. Focus is on improving writing through exercises and mindful choices rather than beginner-level instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready when the stories find us / readiness and self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some people see art as a matter of control. I see it mostly as a matter of self-control.... If I can keep myself, my ego, my wishes and opinions, my mental junk, out of the way and find the focus of the story, and follow the movement of the story, the story will tell itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare by learning craft and skills so you can recognize and guide a story when it arrives; cultivate self-control and the ability to defer personal ego to the needs and movement of the story. This is framed as a prerequisite for doing good work rather than a technical trick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust sound and syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin covers how to adjust sound and syntax as core sentence-level craft work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentences for their sound and syntactic shape; use examples and exercises to train sensitivity to rhythm, cadence, and sentence structure. The book assumes some prior familiarity and often demonstrates through succinct examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marshal adjectives and adverbs (manage modifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how to marshal adjectives and adverbs and when modifiers are serving the story versus getting in the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for overuse or weak modifiers; prefer precise, necessary modifiers. Le Guin gives blunt anti-patterns (e.g., the adjective/qualifier 'fucking' described as a big tick) to illustrate careless modifier use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control verb tense and choose tense by story needs
rubrics_metrics.description: “I see the big difference between the past and present tenses not as immediacy but as complexity and size of field... A story told in the present tense is necessarily focused on action in a single time and therefore a single place. Use of the past tense(s) allows continual referring back and forth in time and space.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select past or present tense based on the scope and needs of the story (present = narrow, immediate field; past = broader temporal/spatial field). Avoid following trends (e.g., present tense being 'in vogue') when the story's demands point elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and choose point of view carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin defines six different points of view (first person, limited third person, involved/omniscient author, detached author, observer-narrator in first person and third person) and describes advantages and limitations of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate POV by its affordances and constraints; Le Guin's method: rewrite a small scene in each POV to feel how it works. Use such comparative exercises to select the POV that best serves perspective, intimacy, information control, and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowding and leaping (manage density and white space)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'crowding' Le Guin means keeping the story full, moving, interconnected, rich with echoes; 'leaping' means providing white space and silence around words and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance: maintain narrative momentum and internal richness (crowding) while deliberately inserting pauses, silence, and breathing room (leaping). Avoid wandering into irrelevancies; also avoid constant textual density with no relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by doing: use exercises / 'consciousness-raisers'
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin describes the book as a workbook and calls the exercises 'consciousness-raisers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop technique through practice—structured exercises are central. The reviewer rates these exercises highly and recommends sequencing them with other workshop texts for a self-directed course. Exercises are both diagnostic and skill-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run and participate in successful peer critique groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin provides an entire chapter with useful guidance on how to run a successful peer critique group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow explicit procedures and norms for critique groups (as advised by Le Guin) to create productive feedback environments. Use the chapter as a practical manual for organizing and conducting group critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak filler words and thoughtless phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of anti-patterns: 'Somehow' as a 'super-weasel' (a word that betrays the author didn't bother thinking out the story); careless qualifiers and misapplied passive voice admonitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of convenience words that mask vague thinking; identify and excise 'weasel' words and lazy qualifiers. Also, be precise about grammatical concepts (e.g., don't dogmatically avoid passive voice if you don't understand what it is).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the rules — and know when to break them
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin: 'good and careful writers will blow all Rules of Writing into bits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn prescriptive rules so you can break them intentionally and effectively. Rule-breaking is allowed but should be a conscious, craft-informed choice rather than ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward plotting: steering vs. following the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin takes a neutral stance on plotter vs. pantser: the 'story boat is a magic one... The job of the person at the helm is to help it find its own way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether you plan or discover, your craft role is to guide and refine the story's course—support discovery with craft skills rather than enforcing a one-size-fits-all process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness for audience / skill level (not for beginners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Le Guin warns that her book is 'not for beginners' and the reviewer agrees; the text assumes prior knowledge of basic craft topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the resource against the writer's experience: this material is aimed at writers who already understand basic concepts (tense, POV, sentence mechanics) and are ready for more demanding exercises and terse examples.
